label: paragraph_title
content: Today's Lecture

label: text
content: Today serves as as an outlook of things we can do once we have mapped/aligned ou sequencing reads to the reference genome. We will focus on a specific topic: using whole genome sequencing (WGS) data for the identification of differences between the sequenced genome and the reference genome, so called "variants". However, we will only scratch the surface; the topic is mouch more complex and varied than illustrated here!

label: text
content: But before, let's have a very brief look at some things that we can do but won't discuss today:

label: text
content: - In case of ChIP-seq data: peak calling

label: text
content: - In case of RNA-seq data: measure gene expression, identify alternative splicing

label: text
content: - In case of Hi-C data: identify chromatin interaction

label: paragraph_title
content: ChIP-seq: peak calling

label: paragraph_title
content: ChIP-seq = **chromatin** **immuno** **recipitation** followed by next generation **sequencing**

label: text
content: Basic idea: don't sequence DNA fragments from the entire genome, but only DNA fragments to which a specific protein (e.g., TP53) has bound!

label: text
content: Mapped reads are concentrated around specific DNA regions, only "random noise" for the rest of the genome

label: text
content: - (Usually two peaks that can be merged)

label: text
content: - Statistical "peak calling" to identify the bound DNA regions

label: paragraph_title
content: RNA-seq: gene expression and splicing

label: paragraph_title
content: RNA-seq = RNA sequencing (see for example: Wang et al., 2009)

label: text
content: - Basic idea: sequence RNA molecules instead of genomic DNA (actually: RNA copied into "complementary DNA"=cDNA, which is then sequenced)

label: text
content: - Mapped reads are concentrated in exonic regions which are present in transcribed, mature RNA molecules (e.g., protein-coding messenger RNA)

label: text
content: - Genes with higher read coverage have higher expression levels (more copies of the RNA = more fragments!)

label: text
content: - Reads can "span" splice junctions, e.g., they can start in one exon and end in another

label: vision_footnote
content: MacArthur lab (Massachusetts General Hospital); https://macarthurlab.org

label: text
content: Example: aberrant splicing due to a mutation in the NEB gene; the "Sashimi" plot shows the read coverage over exonic regions and the numbers of splice-junction spanning reads in a control sample (top) and a patient (bottom)

label: paragraph_title
content: Hi-C: identification of chromatin interactions

label: paragraph_title
content: Hi-C is a chromosome conformation capture method (Lieberman-Aiden et al, 2009)

label: text
content: - Basic idea: fuse two genomic regions which interact, then sequence a read pair spanning the artificial junction (one read from each region)

label: text
content: - Mapped reads are concentrated in regions which interacted; each read pair indicates two specific interacting regions

label: text
content: - Output: two-dimensional interaction maps

label: text
content: - The number of read pairs obtained for two regions depends on the interaction frequency

label: paragraph_title
content: Why variant calling?

label: text
content: Variant calling is one of the key challenges in many areas of genomics research and diagnostics. Having aligned the fragments from DNA sequencing of one or more individuals to a reference genome, "single-nulceotide variant (SNV) calling" identifies variable sites, whereas "genotype calling" determines the genotype for each individual at each site (heterozygous SNV, homozygous SNV?). Also structural variants (such as copy-number changes or translocations) can be identified.

label: text
content: - We assume to have data from whole genome sequencing (WGS), not whole exome sequencing (WES)

label: text
content: - WES works similarly for SNV calling, but poses many difficulties for the identification of structural variants

label: text
content: - In the following we will only scratch the surface of the topic ...

label: paragraph_title
content: SNPs and SNVs

label: text
content: - SNP: Single-nucleotide polymorphism. A variant that is polymorphic within a population (pronounced "snip")

label: text
content: By convention: called SNP if present in at least 1% of the population; otherwise it's a "rare variant"

label: text
content: - SNV: Single-nucleotide variant. A variant identified in an individual genome

label: text
content: A "called" SNV can be a SNP (somatic SNVs in tumor samples need not be SNPs)

label: text
content: In medical genomics, we're often interested in SNVs that are not known as SNPs (e.g., rare variants)

label: text
content: (However, except for tumor samples, the terms "SNP" and "SNV" often are used interchangeably)

label: text
content: About 3-4 million SNVs in a typical genome! Several thousand SNVs in a typical exome ( $ \approx $ 1% of genome)!

content: A naive algorithm

label: text
content: For germline variants, the frequency heuristic works reasonably well if the sequencing depth/coverage is high (large enough n for most genomic positions), so that the probability of a heterozygous nucleotide falling outside of the 20% - 80% region is low. (For somatic variants in cancer we can also have lower frequencies!)

label: text
content: Problems with the frequency heuristic:

label: text
content: - For low sequencing depth (and hence low n), it leads to undercalling of heterozygous genotypes

label: text
content: Example: 2 out of 6 reads (33%) would be interpreted as a heterozygous mutation, 1 out of 6 reads (17%) would be homozygous reference (no variant at all), but is this actually a significant difference considering a random sampling process?

label: text
content: - Also: a changed base on a single read can also be a sequencing error

label: text
content: Possible solution: require a minimum number of reads $ (n)_{min} $ and a minimum number of ALT bases $ (n-k)_{min}! $

label: text
content: ★ Problem here: we may have many locations in the genome for which these thresholds aren't reached and we cannot tell whether there are variants or not ...

label: text
content: - Use of a binary (yes/no) base quality filter leads to loss of information

label: text
content: - Are the reads hinting at an alternate base those with the lowest mapping quality and/or lowest base quality at that position?

label: text
content: - The approach does not provide a measure of confidence in the genotype call

label: text
content: How likely is the predicted genotype/variant to be true?

label: text
content: In Bayesian statistics, maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation is often used to generate an estimate of the maximum value of a probability distribution.

label: text
content: That is, if x is used to refer to the data (x can be an arbitrary expression), and $ \theta $ is used to refer to the parameters of a model, then Bayes' law states that:

label: display_formula
text
content: The term $ P(\theta|x) $ is referred to as the posterior probability, and specifies the probability of the parameters $ \theta $ given the observed data x. The denominator on the right-hand side, $ P(x) $ , can be regarded as a normalizing constant that does not depend on $ \theta $ , and so it can be disregarded for the maximization of $ \theta $ .

label: text

\hat {\theta} = \underset {\theta} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} P (\theta | x) = \underset {\theta} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} P (x | \theta) P (\theta)
$$

label: text
content: For instance, if the alignment at position u has one mismatch with PHRED base quality 20 and one with PHRED quality 10, then

label: paragraph_title
content: MAQ: mapping and base quality

label: text
content: We now calculate the posterior probability $ p_{s}\left(u|\mathcal{R},z\right) $ that read z actually maps to position u, using Bayes' law

label: display_formula
text
content: - MAQ actually uses various heuristics to calculate the mapping error probability, an thus the the mapping quality of read $z$, resulting in a Phred-scaled score $Q_{z}$ for the probability that the read is wrongly mapped

label: text
content: - MAQ then redefines base qualities as the minimum of base quality $ Q_{i} $ and mapping quality $ Q_{z} $ :

label: display_formula
content:
$$
Q _ {i} = \min \left(Q _ {i}, Q _ {z}\right)
$$

label: text
content: Rationale: if a base has a high base quality (confident sequencing result) but we're not sure whether the read actually comes from that genomic region (low mapping quality), we shouldn't give much emphasis on what the base tells us about the position to which is has (maybe wrongly) been mapped

label: text
content: The inverse is also true: if we are very confident about the mapping of a read, but not about the quality of the individual base, then the information of this read for this particular position in the genome should be taken with caution!

label: display_formula

label: paragraph_title
content: Correction for multiple testing

label: text
content: We are making millions of tests across the genome (millions of windows!) ..

label: text
content: - For each test we compute a p-value: a probability that the "null hypothesis" (no particular event) is true

label: text
content: - Usually, we say we "reject" the null hypothesis if $ p < 0.05 $ (we consider this to be an interesting event!)

label: text
content: - But: the probability that we are wrong is $p!$

label: vision_footnote
content: If you make millions of tests, some p-values will just by chance be low enough without constituting true events ...

label: paragraph_title
content: Correction for multiple testing

label: text
content: The p-value is the probability, under the null hypothesis, that the test statistic assumes the observed or a more extreme value.

label: text
content: It is important to realize that if we go on testing long enough, we will inevitably find something which appears "significant" by chance alone.

label: text
content: - If we test a null hypothesis that is true (= no significant event) using a significance level of $ \alpha=0. 0 5 $ , then there is a probability of $ 1-\alpha=0. 9 5 $ of arriving at a correct conclusion of non-significance

label: text
content: If we now test two independent true null hypotheses, the probability that neither test appears significant is $ 0.95\times0.95=0.90 $

label: text
content: - If we test 50 independent null hypotheses, the probability that none will appear significant is then $ ( 0.95 )^{50}=0.077 $ (only 7.7%)

label: text
content: This corresponds to a probability of $ 1-0.077=0.923 $ of getting at least one spurious "significant" result even of there is no true event(!), and the expected number of spurious significant results in 50 tests is $ 50\times 0.05=2.5 $

label: text
content: These are called "false positives" (we consider them relevant, but they are not!)

label: text
content: Multiple-testing correction (MTC) procedures have been developed to limit the probability of false-positive results.

label: paragraph_title
content: Correction for multiple testing

label: text
content: The most stringent MTC is the Bonferroni procedure.

label: text
content: - Probability of non-significant result for a single test if the null hypothesis is true $ \Leftrightarrow 1-\alpha $

label: text
content: - Probability of getting no significant result for k such tests is $ (1 - \alpha)^{k} $

label: text
content: - If we make $ \alpha $ small enough, then we can make $ (1-\alpha)^{k}=0.95 $ (corresponding to overall $ \alpha $ level of 5%, i.e., with a 95% we have not a single false positive among the k tests!)

label: text
content: - If $ \alpha $ is very small, then $ (1-\alpha)^{k}\approx 1-k\alpha $

label: text
content: - Therefore, the Bonferroni sets $ \alpha=\frac{1-0.95}{k} $

label: text
content: - Thus, instead of accepting each result with a $ p $ -value of $ p < 0.05 $ , we accept only results with $ p < \frac{0.05}{k} $ where k is the number of tests we make

label: text
content: - Note: this, in contrast to other MTC procedures, is very restrictive and may thus lead to a high number of "false negatives" (true events which we don't recognize as such)
